Q: C# Blazor using SQLite - DllNotFoundException A:

The first result in a Google search for sqlite is SQLite Home Page. If one visits SQLite Home Page and clicks Download one is presented with a web page that shows various downloads. It appears that one has numerous options.

You stated that you're using .NET 10 LTS. According to An introduction to NuGet:

For .NET (including .NET Core), the Microsoft-supported mechanism for sharing code is NuGet, which defines how packages for .NET are created, hosted, and consumed, and provides the tools for each of those roles.

Going back to the SQLite Download web page if one looks under the heading Precompiled Binaries for .NET one sees

See the System.Data.SQLite.org website.

Upon navigating to System.Data.SQLite.org website one sees the following:

System.Data.SQLite is an ADO.NET provider for SQLite.

How to use this library System.Data.SQLite is available on nuget.org. Typical usage would involve adding two packages, one for System.Data.SQLite, and one containing a native build of SQLite. For example:

<ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference id="System.Data.SQLite" version="2.0.3"/>
    <PackageReference id="SourceGear.sqlite3" version="3.50.4.5"/>
</ItemGroup>

According to the documentation one should download/install two Nuget packages:

  • System.Data.SQLite (you may try using Microsoft.Data.SQLite instead)
  • SourceGear.sqlite3

Q: How to hide includes from other classes? A:

First off, think using headers and translation units, not using classes. You can't "include a class" whether in a header, TU or another class.

I'm not sure if you only want to constrain visibility or actually make Table agnostic of any details of InternalData. If it's the latter, you want to eat your cake and have it too. If Table has a data member of type InternalData, you need to know about what InternalData is, that's a fundamental limitation of programming language design in general.

C++ wasn't originally designed to provide elegant solutions to minor problems that can have not-too-ugly hatchet solutions (PIMPL). Since C++20, you can use modules, which let you define your source-level visibility rules through import/export.

In general, however, don't expect any programming language to always have elegant solutions to your problems. There are always trade-offs.

Q: PowerShell script error. Why is the string element's Count method being referenced and not the array's Count method? A:

Preface:

  • You're defining (and calling) a .Count() method on your custom class, which is distinct from the standard .Count property that PowerShell surfaces for .NET arrays.

  • As such, your .Count method definition doesn't override anything (unlike your .ToString() definition).

    • As Santiago notes, PowerShell classes do not support computed properties (property getters), so you cannot directly override the .Count property as intended.
    • A - cumbersome - workaround, as noted, is to use PowerShell's ETS (Extended Type System) to define a ScriptProperty and attach it instances of your custom class: see this answer for an example.
      GitHub issue #2219 proposes adding support for property getters/setters in a future PowerShell version

The next section explains why your .Count() method call didn't work as expected.

The problem is most likely:

  • The $ScrsPath variable (whose initialization you're not showing) is defined with a [string[]] type constraint, as typically happens with parameter variables.

    • With a regular variable, such a type constraint would look something like this:
      [string[]] $SrcsPaths = @('c:\tmp\scr1', 'c:\tmp\scr2')
      Notably, any subsequent assignment to $SrcsPaths (that doesn't use a type constraint) coerces the assigned value back to [string[]][1]

  • As a result, your attempt to change the type of $ScrsPath from [string[]] to an instance of your custom class, [StringArray] by mere assignment - in effect, $SrcsPath = [StringArray]::new( $SrcsPath ) - fails, because the assigned value is uselessly coerced back to a [string[]] instance[1], which doesn't have a .Count method and neither do its [string] elements:[2] hence the error.

The immediate fix is to use a type constraint again, with the desired new type, i.e. [StringArray]:

$myArray = [StringArray]::new( $SrcsPath )  
# Note the [StringArray] type constraint.
[StringArray] $SrcsPath = $myArray  
$myArray = $Null

Taking a step back:

  • It is precisely such subtleties involving type-constrained variables that makes it advisable not to repurpose them - use a different variable instead.

  • Additionally, from a code-maintenance perspective, changing the type of a variable in the body of a script or function can be confusing.

Thus, if you had used a different variable to store your [StringArray] instance, you wouldn't have had to worry about ensuring use of a type constraint; to wit:

# Create the [StringArray] instance in a new variable, and use
# the latter below.
$ScrsPathCustom = [StringArray]::new( $SrcsPath )  

Write-Host -ForegroundColor White "`$SrcsPathCustom: $SrcsPathCustom (" + $SrcsPathCustom.Count() + ")"

[1] What happens is that a scalar RHS' string representation becomes the one and only element of the resulting [string[]] array; a simple example: [string[]] $arr = Get-Date is in effect the same as $arr = [string[]]::new(1); $arr[0] = (Get-Date).ToString()

[2] Specifically, when PowerShell cannot find a requested method on an enumerable such as an array, it looks for it on the enumerable's individual elements, a feature known as member-access enumeration.

Q: How to change $_ value before condition check A:

I suggest simplifying your code as follows, which also bypasses your problem:

$ADUsers | Where-Object {
  [guid]::new($_.msExchMailboxGuid) -eq $mb.ExchangeGuid
}

  • Update: As iRon points out in a comment on the question - assuming that $_.msExchMailboxGuid truly contains a [byte[]] array - simply swapping operands should suffice, given that PowerShell typically coerces the RHS operand to the LHS operand's type, if they differ; therefore:

    # LHS is of type [guid], so the [byte[]] RHS is coerced to [guid] too.
$ADUsers | Where-Object { $mb.ExchangeGuid -eq $_.msExchMailboxGuid }
    • See this answer for more information, as well as this answer for details about PowerShell's surprisingly flexible implicit type conversions.[1]

While I cannot recreate the exact symptom, the problem with your approach is the mistaken use of $(...), the subexpression operator, in your
New-Object Guid @(,$($_.msExchMailboxGuid)) call (there are additional, superfluous uses in your code, which add unnecessary overhead but are otherwise benign):

  • The correct syntax would be New-Object Guid (, $_.msExchMailboxGuid) - which is the equivalent of the [guid]::new($_.msExchMailboxGuid) call above, which uses the intrinsic ::new() method for calling constructors.
    The [byte[]] instance stored in $_.msExchMailboxGuid causes selection of the relevant constructor overload of type System.Guid.

    • As for why (, $_.msExchMailboxGuid) rather than just $_.msExchMailboxGuid is needed as the second positional New-Object argument, see this answer.

  • In expressions, $(...) is rarely the right tool: its primary purpose is to embed expressions and statements in expandable (interpolating) strings (double-quoted, i.e. inside "...")

    • See this answer for background information.

  • In the case at hand, $(...) enumerates the elements of the [byte[]] array stored in $_.msExchMailboxGuid and then re-collects them in an [object[]] array, as a result of which New-Object cannot identify the relevant constructor overload.

[1] A simple demonstration of the fact that PowerShell implicitly converts a [byte[]] RHS operand to [guid], if that is the LSH operand's type, by way of [guid] providing a single-argument constructor that accepts [byte[]]:
[guid]::Empty -eq [guid]::Empty.ToByteArray() yields $true.
